```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_torch <- torch::torch_is_installed()
```

```{r setup}
library(graphlearnR)
```

Many graphs have more than one kind of node and edge: authors write papers,
drugs target proteins, users rate items. A heterogeneous graph keeps each
node type with its own feature space and each relation with its own edges, so
a model can learn relation specific transformations.

## Building one

Node types are given as a named list; each entry is a feature matrix, a list
with `x`, `y`, and masks, or just a node count for types without features.
Relations are keyed `"source__relation__target"`. Indices are 1-based
*within each type*, so `author__writes__paper` edge `(2, 3)` means author 2
wrote paper 3.

```{r}
hg <- hetero_graph_data(
  nodes = list(
    author = list(x = matrix(rnorm(8), 4, 2), y = factor(c("ml", "db", "ml", "db"))),
    paper = matrix(rnorm(15), 5, 3),
    venue = 2
  ),
  edges = list(
    author__writes__paper = rbind(c(1, 1, 2, 3, 4), c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)),
    paper__cites__paper = rbind(c(2, 3, 5), c(1, 1, 4)),
    paper__published_in__venue = rbind(1:5, c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2))
  )
)
hg
edge_types(hg)
```

Indices are checked against the size of their own node type, and the error
names the relation and the side.

```{r}
try(hetero_graph_data(nodes = list(a = diag(2), b = diag(3)),
                      edges = list(a__r__b = rbind(3, 1))))
```

### Reverse relations

Messages flow along edge direction. Without a reverse of
`author__writes__paper`, papers would never send information to authors.
`add_reverse_relations()` adds `paper__rev_writes__author` and records the
pairing, which the link splitter uses to prevent leakage.

```{r}
hg <- add_reverse_relations(hg)
edge_types(hg)[, c("key", "reverse")]
```

### Homogeneous view

`to_homogeneous()` places every type in one index space with offsets, pads
features to a common width, and records the original type of each node and
edge. This is useful for exporting to tools that do not know about types.

```{r}
flat <- to_homogeneous(hg, target_type = "author")
flat
flat$metadata$type_ptr
table(flat$edge_type)
```

## A worked example: drug classes

`dataset_synthetic_hetero()` simulates drugs that target proteins and
proteins that interact. A drug's class is determined by the proteins it
targets more than by its own features, so a model must pass messages across
the relation.

```{r}
dh <- add_reverse_relations(dataset_synthetic_hetero(seed = 1))
dh
```

`hetero_gnn_model()` builds one convolution per relation and per layer and
sums (or averages) the results that arrive at each node type. Node types
without features get a learned embedding.

```{r, eval = has_torch}
library(torch)
results <- list()
for (cv in c("sage", "graph_conv", "gat", "rgcn", "hgt")) {
  torch_manual_seed(1)
  m <- hetero_gnn_model(dh, hidden_dim = 32, output_dim = 3, target_type = "drug",
                        conv = cv, dropout = 0.2)
  fit <- train_graph_model(m, dh, "node_classification", target_type = "drug",
                           epochs = 80, lr = 0.01, seed = 1)
  ev <- evaluate_graph_model(fit, dh)
  results[[cv]] <- ev$value[ev$metric == "accuracy"]
}
unlist(results)
```

`conv = "rgcn"` shares bases across relations when `num_bases` is set,
which helps when there are many relations with few edges each.

`conv = "hgt"` uses heterogeneous graph transformer layers (Hu et al.
2020), see `hgt_conv()`. Keys, queries and values are projected with
weights per node type, each relation has its own attention and message
matrices, and the attention softmax at a node runs over all its incoming
edges across relations, so relations compete for attention. The relative
temporal encoding of the paper is not implemented.

```{r, eval = has_torch}
layer <- hgt_conv(dh$node_types, names(dh$edges), 8, 8, heads = 2)
ht <- hetero_tensors(dh)
x <- list(drug = torch_randn(60, 8), protein = torch_randn(80, 8))
out <- layer(x, ht$edge_index)
lapply(out, dim)
a <- layer$last_attention$protein
summary(as.numeric(scatter_sum(a$alpha, a$index, 80)$sum(dim = 2)))
```

The last line sums the attention each protein gives to its neighbors per
head; every protein with incoming edges gets exactly one per head, which
is 2 here.

## Relation specific link prediction

`split_edges_hetero()` splits one relation. Held out edges are removed both
from that relation and from its reverse, otherwise the model could read a
test edge backwards during message passing. Negatives are drawn with the
source from the source type and the target from the target type.

```{r}
sp <- split_edges_hetero(dh, "drug__targets__protein", val = 0.1, test = 0.2, seed = 2)
sp
held <- paste(sp$test_pos[1, ], sp$test_pos[2, ])
rev <- sp$train_graph$edges$protein__rev_targets__drug$edge_index
any(paste(rev[2, ], rev[1, ]) %in% held)
```

```{r, eval = has_torch}
torch_manual_seed(2)
m <- hetero_gnn_model(dh, hidden_dim = 32, conv = "sage", dropout = 0)
fit_l <- train_graph_model(m, sp, "link_prediction", epochs = 60, seed = 2)
evaluate_graph_model(fit_l)
```

## Typed neighbor sampling

`sample_hetero_neighbors()` samples incoming edges of every relation hop by
hop, starting from seeds of one or more types. Fanouts can be one number per
hop for all relations, or a named list per relation; a relation left out of
the list is not sampled.

```{r}
sg <- sample_hetero_neighbors(dh, seeds = list(drug = c(1, 2)), fanouts = c(3, 2),
                              seed = 1)
lengths(sg$n_id)
vapply(sg$edges, function(e) ncol(e$edge_index), integer(1))
```

Local indices map back through `sg$n_id[[type]]`, just as in the homogeneous
sampler.

## Batching

`hetero_batch()` combines heterogeneous graphs with the same schema, offsetting
indices separately for every node type and recording a `batch` vector per
type.

```{r}
hb <- hetero_batch(list(hg, hg))
num_nodes(hb)
hb$batch$author
```
